body:
From bedrock to soil

Weathering provides much of the mineral material from which soils develop. However, loose weathered rock fragments alone do not constitute a fully developed soil.

Regolith is the loose or unconsolidated material covering consolidated bedrock. It may include weathered rock fragments, transported sediments and soil. Soil is the biologically and chemically active near-surface material containing mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms.

The process of soil formation and development is called pedogenesis.

Physical weathering reduces particle size. Chemical weathering alters the original minerals and may generate secondary minerals such as clay. Plants, microorganisms and animals add organic matter and mix the developing soil.

Partially decomposed and transformed organic matter contributes to humus. Humus supports soil structure, nutrient retention and biological activity. Plant roots and soil organisms also help develop pores through which air and water move.

Factors of soil formation

Soil formation depends on 5 major interacting factors.

FactorInfluence on soil formation
Parent materialInfluences mineral composition, texture and initial chemical properties
ClimateControls moisture, temperature, weathering and leaching
OrganismsContribute organic matter, decomposition and mixing
Relief or topographyInfluences drainage, erosion and material accumulation
TimeAllows weathering, biological activity and soil horizons to develop

Parent material and topography are commonly described as passive soil-forming factors, while climate and biological activity are active factors. Time governs the duration over which these influences operate.

Parent material alone cannot determine every property of a soil. The same type of rock can produce different soils under different climates and drainage conditions.

Soil horizons

As a soil develops, biological activity and the movement of water and minerals may produce distinct layers called horizons. A vertical section showing these layers is called a soil profile.

Horizon or layerGeneral characteristic
OSurface organic material, where present
AMineral topsoil commonly enriched with organic matter
EZone of pronounced material removal, where developed
BSubsoil showing alteration or accumulation of transported constituents
CRelatively weakly altered parent material
RUnderlying hard bedrock

Not every soil contains all these horizons. Their development depends on environmental conditions and the stage of soil formation.

The downward or outward removal of material from a soil horizon is called eluviation. Its accumulation within another horizon is called illuviation. Leaching refers particularly to the removal of soluble substances by percolating water.

Residual and transported soils

Residual soils

Residual soils develop from weathered parent material that remains substantially at its original location. Their mineral characteristics may therefore reflect the underlying rock, particularly during earlier stages of development.

Transported soils

Transported soils develop from material carried from another location by water, wind, glaciers or gravity. Their parent material may have little direct relationship with the local bedrock.

Alluvial soils develop from river-deposited sediments. Wind-deposited silt may provide the parent material for soils developed on loess deposits.

Important Indian and Gujarat relationships

Basalt and black soil

Weathering of basaltic rocks has contributed to extensive black soil development in the Deccan region, including parts of Gujarat. Black soils are commonly clay-rich, retain considerable moisture and may develop deep cracks during dry periods because of the shrinkage of clay minerals.

Black soil is also known as regur or black cotton soil. Although its association with basalt is important, black soils do not occur exclusively on basaltic bedrock.

Intense weathering and lateritic materials

Under warm conditions with abundant rainfall and effective drainage, prolonged chemical weathering may remove considerable amounts of soluble constituents and silica. Iron and aluminium compounds may become relatively concentrated in the remaining material.

This process contributes to lateritic soil and rock development. Under suitable geological conditions, weathering may also produce economically important bauxite concentrations.

Alluvial plains of Gujarat

River-deposited sediments provide important parent materials for soils in Gujarat's alluvial plains. Their characteristics reflect the sediments supplied by rivers as well as local climate, drainage, organisms and time.

Soil formation and soil conservation

Soil formation is generally slow compared with the rapid removal that can occur during severe erosion. Vegetation cover, contour ploughing, appropriately constructed terraces, mulching and controlled runoff help conserve soil by reducing its removal.

Prelims focus

  • Pedogenesis means soil formation.
  • The 5 major soil-forming factors are parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time.
  • Eluviation is removal from a horizon; illuviation is accumulation in another horizon.
  • Regur is black soil, not a rock family.
  • Residual soil develops in place; alluvial soil develops from transported sediment.
  • Trap: All regolith is not soil, and soil properties are not determined by parent rock alone.

[References: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 13-14; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Soil Formation and Soil-forming Factors; NCERT, Contemporary India-I, Class 9, Physical Features of India, Peninsular Plateau; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 39-40. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Weathering, Regolith and Soil Formation

body:
Meaning of mass wasting

Gravity acts continuously on rocks, soil and loose materials lying on slopes. When the forces tending to move these materials downslope exceed their resistance to movement, part of the slope may become unstable and move.

Mass wasting, also called mass movement, is the downslope movement of rock, soil or debris primarily under the direct influence of gravity.

Mass wasting differs from erosion by rivers, wind or glaciers because those agents do not have to carry the material during a mass movement. Water can assist mass wasting by increasing the weight of slope materials and reducing their resistance to movement.

Weathering commonly promotes mass movement by loosening rocks and producing debris. However, weathering is not an essential prerequisite. Even relatively unweathered rock can move if a fracture, earthquake or other disturbance causes slope failure.

Classification of mass movements

Mass movements are distinguished by their speed, the material involved, the amount of moisture present and the manner in which the material moves.

Soil creep

Creep is an extremely slow downslope movement of soil or weathered material. Repeated expansion and contraction associated with wetting and drying, freezing and thawing, or other disturbances can gradually shift particles downhill.

Although individual movements are difficult to observe, their cumulative effects may appear as tilted fence posts, bent tree trunks, distorted retaining structures or small surface ridges.

Solifluction

Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil or weathered material. It is particularly associated with cold environments where a seasonally thawed surface layer becomes saturated above frozen or poorly permeable ground.

When drainage is restricted, the wet material can gradually move downslope under gravity.

Earthflow, mudflow and debris flow

A flow occurs when slope material undergoes substantial internal deformation and moves in a manner resembling a viscous fluid.

  • Earthflow: Movement dominated by relatively fine-grained earth material, often containing considerable moisture.
  • Mudflow: Flow dominated by wet, fine-grained material and water.
  • Debris flow: Flow containing a mixture of water, soil and coarser rock fragments. It can move rapidly through valleys or channels.
  • Debris avalanche: An exceptionally rapid movement of a mass of fragmented rock and debris.

Flows differ from slides because the moving material experiences substantial internal rearrangement rather than remaining primarily as a coherent mass.

Slides and slumps

In a slide, a mass of rock or soil moves along a recognisable surface of failure.

A translational slide moves along a relatively planar surface, such as an inclined bedding plane, joint or fault.

A rotational slide, commonly called a slump, moves along a curved failure surface. The sliding mass typically undergoes backward rotation as it moves downslope.

Rockfall and toppling

Rockfall occurs when rock fragments detach from a steep or overhanging slope and descend through falling, bouncing or rolling. The fragments may accumulate at the foot of the slope as angular debris called scree or talus.

Toppling involves forward rotation of a rock mass away from a slope before or during its collapse.

Comparison of common mass movements

MovementTypical rateIdentifying feature
CreepVery slowGradual displacement of soil
SolifluctionSlowFlow of saturated surface material
EarthflowVariableDeformation of fine-grained earth
Debris flowOften rapidFlow of water and mixed debris
Translational slideVariableMovement along a relatively planar surface
SlumpVariableCurved failure surface and rotation
RockfallRapidDetachment from a steep rock face

Landslides and mass wasting

The term landslide is widely used for slope failures involving rock, debris or earth. In modern geological hazard classification, it encompasses several forms of movement, including slides, falls, topples and flows. Some school-level classifications use the term more narrowly for relatively rapid sliding and related slope failures.

Mass wasting is the broader geomorphic concept and includes extremely slow movements such as soil creep as well as sudden failures.

Prelims focus

  • Gravity is the principal driving force of mass wasting.
  • Creep is an extremely slow downslope movement.
  • Solifluction is associated with water-saturated soil, particularly in cold environments.
  • Slump involves movement along a curved failure surface with rotation.
  • Rockfall may produce scree or talus at the base of a slope.
  • Trap: Neither prior weathering nor the presence of water is compulsory for every mass movement.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Mass Movements, Slow Movements, Rapid Movements and Landslides; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 12; US Geological Survey, Landslide Types and Processes, Fact Sheet 2004-3072; US Geological Survey, What Is a Landslide and What Causes One? Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Why slopes become unstable

The stability of a slope depends on the relationship between forces tending to move material downhill and the strength of the material resisting that movement. Resistance is provided by friction, cohesion between particles, the strength of the rock and the arrangement of geological structures.

A slope fails when the forces promoting downslope movement exceed the available resistance. Both natural processes and human activities can disturb this balance.

Factors increasing landslide susceptibility

Slope gradient and geological structure

Steep slopes experience a stronger tendency for material to move downhill than gentle slopes, other conditions being similar.

Loose sediments, weak rocks, deeply weathered materials and highly fractured rocks are often susceptible to failure. Bedding planes, joints and faults may provide surfaces along which a mass can slide. Rock layers inclined outward towards a slope face may create particularly favourable conditions for sliding.

Heavy rainfall and water saturation

Prolonged or intense rainfall can infiltrate soil and rock fractures. Water saturation may increase the weight of slope material and raise the pressure of water within its pores.

Increased pore-water pressure reduces the effective contact forces between particles and may reduce their frictional resistance. Some clay-rich materials also weaken when wet. These effects can promote slope failure.

Removal of support at the slope base

Rivers, waves or human excavation may remove material from the foot of a slope. The removal of this supporting material is called undercutting. It can leave the upper portion unsupported and vulnerable to collapse.

Earthquakes and other disturbances

Earthquake shaking can destabilise rock masses and loose slope materials. Volcanic activity, natural changes in groundwater conditions and sudden changes in river or reservoir water levels may also trigger failures in susceptible terrain.

Vegetation removal

Plant roots can help bind shallow soil, while vegetation can intercept rainfall and influence soil moisture. Indiscriminate deforestation may increase erosion and reduce the stability of some shallow slopes.

Vegetation cannot prevent every landslide. Deep-seated failures or movement of large fractured rock masses may require geological and engineering measures beyond vegetation restoration.

Human activities that can increase risk

  • Unplanned cutting of steep slopes for roads and buildings.
  • Excavation or quarrying that removes essential support.
  • Excessive loading of a slope with construction material or waste.
  • Inadequate drainage that allows water to accumulate or infiltrate susceptible materials.
  • Removal of protective vegetation and disturbance of natural drainage.

Landslide-prone regions of India

The Himalayan region

The Himalayas are highly susceptible to landslides because of their steep relief, tectonic activity, fractured rocks, locally unconsolidated deposits and heavy rainfall or snowmelt in many areas. River incision and road construction may increase instability.

The Western Ghats and Nilgiri hills

The Western Ghats and Nilgiris are relatively tectonically stable compared with the Himalayas, but their steep escarpments, deeply weathered materials in some areas and intense monsoon rainfall create considerable landslide susceptibility.

The occurrence of landslides in these regions demonstrates that active tectonics is not a necessary condition for slope failure.

Other susceptible terrain

Parts of northeastern India and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also contain terrain susceptible to slope failure. Local geological structure, rainfall, relief and human disturbance determine the distribution and severity of hazards within each region.

In Gujarat, slope stability remains locally relevant wherever steep hill slopes, natural rock escarpments, quarry faces and road cuttings occur. Statewide risk should not be inferred merely from the presence of a particular rock type.

Consequences of landslides

Landslides can damage settlements, roads, agricultural land, water supply systems and other infrastructure. They may block rivers and temporarily form natural dams. If such a dam fails suddenly, the stored water may produce destructive downstream flooding.

Measures for reducing landslide risk

MeasurePurpose
Hazard zonation and land-use planningIdentify susceptible terrain and avoid unsafe development
Surface and subsurface drainageLimit water accumulation and excessive pore-water pressure
Slope grading and engineered benchesReduce excessive slope steepness where appropriate
Retaining and supporting structuresProvide engineered support to unstable materials
Vegetation restorationReduce surface erosion and improve shallow soil reinforcement
Monitoring and early warningDetect developing instability and support timely protective action

Appropriate measures depend on the nature and depth of the failure, geological conditions, drainage and the activities exposed to the hazard. A retaining wall alone cannot resolve every slope instability problem, especially if excessive water pressure remains uncontrolled.

Prelims focus

  • Heavy rainfall can increase slope weight and reduce resistance through rising pore-water pressure.
  • Undercutting removes support from the base of a slope.
  • The Himalayas, Western Ghats and Nilgiris are important landslide-susceptible regions.
  • Landslide dams can cause downstream flooding if they fail.
  • Drainage, hazard zonation and suitable slope stabilisation help reduce landslide risk.
  • Trap: Landslides occur in tectonically stable regions as well as tectonically active mountain belts.

Overall relationship between rocks and surface processes

Rock origin determines mineral composition and geological structure. These characteristics influence susceptibility to physical and chemical weathering. Weathering produces fragments, altered minerals and regolith that contribute to soil formation. On slopes, loosened materials may move under gravity or be removed by other erosional agents. Subsequent deposition and lithification can produce new sedimentary rocks, linking these surface processes back to the rock cycle.

[References: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 12; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Mass Movements; NCERT, India Physical Environment, Class 11, Natural Hazards and Disasters, Landslides; US Geological Survey, What Is a Landslide and What Causes One?, and Landslide Types and Processes, Fact Sheet 2004-3072. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
